title: Logic: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can explain what logic and critical thinking do: check whether the reasons for a claim really support it.
summary: Logic sorts good arguments from bad by asking whether reasons support a claim. Its name comes from Greek logos. Dewey's reflective thought weighs a belief by the grounds behind it.

cards.headline: "The café must be closed. The lights are off." Good reason?
cards.body: Maybe. Or maybe the owner just likes candlelight. You hear reasons like this all day, from friends, from ads and from your own head. This whole skill is about one question: do the reasons really support the claim?

cards.headline: What logic does
cards.body: Logic studies reasoning. Logic has many uses, and the open textbook forall x focuses on this one: evaluating arguments, sorting the good ones from the bad. It adds that logic might even be called the science of what follows from what. So at the café, logic's question isn't "Is it closed?" It's "Do dark windows get you to closed?" Dark windows and an open door can go together.

cards.fact: "Logic" comes from the Greek logos: word, reason.
cards.context: It reached English through Latin logica, from the Greek logike techne, "the reasoning art". The name fits. Logic works on reasons put into words, the kind you can say out loud, write down and then test.

cards.headline: Critical thinking: logic for everyday life
cards.body: In How We Think, published in 1910, the American philosopher John Dewey described reflective thought: careful consideration of any belief in the light of the grounds that support it. The idea of teaching critical thinking goes back to him. His advice for the café? Hold off deciding until you've looked at the grounds.
cards.callout: Dewey: "The essence of critical thinking is suspended judgment."

learned: Logic sorts good arguments from bad

title: What Counts as an Argument
objective: After this level you can tell an argument, a set of reasons offered for a claim, from a quarrel, a story or a bare opinion.
summary: In logic an argument is reasons offered for a claim, not a quarrel. Monty Python's Argument Clinic makes the point: contradiction isn't an argument.

cards.headline: In a 1972 comedy sketch, a man pays for an argument. He gets contradiction.
cards.body: In Monty Python's "Argument Clinic", everything he says is simply denied. Finally he protests that an argument isn't just contradiction. It's "a connected series of statements" meant to establish a point. Philosophy teachers still show the sketch in class, because he's right.

cards.headline: Two kinds of argument
cards.body: Everyday English uses "argument" for a quarrel. Logic doesn't. The forall x textbook says shouting matches aren't arguments in its sense at all; they're just disagreements. In logic, an argument is reasons offered for a claim. So two people can quarrel for an hour without making a single argument, and one calm person can make an argument alone.

cards.headline: The logician's definition
cards.body: An argument is a set of statements, some of which are offered as reasons for thinking another one is true. "The match is off, because the pitch is flooded" qualifies: one reason, one claim, and a link between them. That link is what the Argument Clinic customer meant by a "connected series". The reasons have a proper name, premises, and Level 5 is all about them.

cards.headline: What isn't an argument
cards.body: A bare opinion isn't one. "Pineapple belongs on pizza!" states a view with no reason attached, and shouting it louder doesn't help. A story isn't one either: "Sam woke up, fed the cat and left" reports events without trying to prove anything. The test: is someone trying to establish a statement as true by basing it on another statement? If not, there's no argument, however heated it gets.

title: Claims: True or False
objective: After this level you can explain what a claim is and why only claims, not questions or commands, can be true or false.
summary: A claim is a sentence that can be true or false, even a false one. Questions, commands and exclamations are neither, so they can't be premises or conclusions.

cards.headline: "Are you sleepy yet?" can't be true. It can't be false either.
cards.body: Try it: nobody answers a question with "False!" But reply "I'm not sleepy", and you've said something that is either true or false. That small difference decides what an argument can be built from.

cards.headline: What a claim is
cards.body: A claim, which logicians also call a statement, is a sentence that can be true or false. "The Nile is a river in northeastern Africa" is a claim, and a true one. "The Yangtze is a river in Japan" is a claim too, just a false one. Being wrong doesn't disqualify a sentence. It only has to be the kind of thing that could be right or wrong.

cards.headline: Questions, commands and ouches
cards.body: Three kinds of sentence can't be true or false. Questions: "Are you sleepy yet?" Commands: "Wake up!" Exclamations: "Ouch!" None of them states how things are, so none of them is a claim. Answer the question, though, and you're back in business. Questions aren't claims; answers are.

cards.headline: Why only claims count
cards.body: Level 2's arguments are built from statements: the reasons and the conclusion are all claims, because an argument tries to show that something is true. A command can't be a conclusion, since nothing could make "Wake up!" true. A claim can still join an argument when it turns out false. What matters is that asking "true or false?" makes sense.

title: Fact, Opinion or Value?
objective: After this level you can sort a statement into a checkable fact, a personal taste or a value judgment.
summary: Factual claims can be checked by observation or research, even when wrong. Opinions of taste have no such check. Value judgments say what ought to be, against a standard.

cards.headline: Three claims about mice. Each one is checked in a different way.
cards.body: "Mice are animals." "Mice make the best pets." "You should feed your pet mouse every day." All three are claims in Level 3's sense. But you'd settle them very differently: one with a biology book, one probably never, and one by asking what we owe the animals we keep.

cards.fact: A factual claim can be checked by observation or research.
cards.context: "Mice are animals" is one. Logicians call such claims descriptive: they say what is in fact the case. A factual claim can also be wrong. "Mice are reptiles" is still a factual claim, just an erroneous one, and any biology book will set it straight.

cards.headline: Taste: no referee
cards.body: "Mice make the best pets" and "Blue is the best color" are opinions. The OpenStax textbook College Success defines an opinion as a statement someone holds to be true without supporting evidence. You can collect facts about mice all day, and a cat lover still won't be proved wrong.

cards.headline: Value judgments: measured against a standard
cards.body: "You should feed your pet mouse every day" is different again. It's a normative claim, or value judgment: it says what ought to be, measured against a standard, such as a moral or a legal one. Words like should, ought, good and bad are the giveaway. To weigh one, first ask which standard it appeals to.

title: Premises and Conclusions
objective: After this level you can name the premises and the conclusion of a simple argument.
summary: Premises are an argument's reasons; the conclusion is the claim they support. 'Premise' means 'set before'. Conclusions can come first, last or in the middle.

cards.headline: "The bakery sells out by noon, and it's one o'clock. The croissants are gone."
cards.body: Sad, but well reasoned. Two claims do the work, and a third is the payoff. Logic has names for those jobs, and once you know them you can take almost any argument apart.

cards.headline: Premises and conclusion
cards.body: The reasons offered in an argument are its premises. The claim they're offered for is its conclusion. At the bakery, "it sells out by noon" and "it's one o'clock" are the premises, and "the croissants are gone" is the conclusion. Every argument needs both: reasons, and something they're reasons for.

cards.fact: "Premise" means "set before". "Conclude" comes from the Latin for "to shut".
cards.context: "Premise" comes from Medieval Latin praemissa, the proposition set before. "Conclusion" comes from Latin concludere, built on claudere, to shut. Premises go first; the conclusion closes the case. A handy memory hook, though real arguments don't always keep that order.

cards.headline: Standard form: lining it up
cards.body: Logicians often rewrite an argument in standard form: number the premises, then put the conclusion last, marked "therefore" or with three dots. 1. The bakery sells out by noon. 2. It's one o'clock. Therefore, the croissants are gone. It looks fussy, but it puts every part where you can see it and question it.

cards.headline: Conclusions don't always come last
cards.body: Everyday speech shuffles the order. "The gardener did it. After all, it was either the butler or the gardener. And the butler didn't do it." Here the conclusion comes first. It can sit in the middle, too, and one sentence can hold a whole argument: "The butler has an alibi; so they cannot have done it." Spotting it is the next level's job.

title: Finding the Conclusion
objective: After this level you can use signal words like "therefore", "so" and "because" to find an argument's conclusion.
summary: So, therefore and thus usually flag a conclusion; because and since flag a reason. They can mislead, so ask which claim the others support.

cards.headline: "So" can point to a conclusion. In "I'm so tired", it points to a nap.
cards.body: Arguments often come with signposts: small words that announce "here's the reason" or "here's the point". Learn to read them and conclusions get much easier to find. Just don't trust every signpost you meet.

cards.headline: Signposts to the conclusion
cards.body: Words like so, therefore, thus, hence, consequently and accordingly usually announce a conclusion. "The pitch is flooded, so the match is off." Whatever follows "so" is the claim being supported. Logicians call these conclusion indicator words.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: "because" introduces the reason, not the conclusion. The conclusion is what the reason supports.

cards.headline: Signposts to a reason
cards.body: Other words flag a premise: because, since, for, as and given that. They point the other way. In "The match is off, because the pitch is flooded", the reason follows "because", so the conclusion sits on the other side of it. Same argument, reversed order, different signpost.

cards.headline: Signposts that mislead
cards.body: Not every "so" or "since" signals an argument. "I have been running competitively since 1999" uses since for time. "I am so happy" uses so for emphasis. Each is one plain claim, with nothing offered as a reason. The word alone never proves there's an argument; the job it's doing does.

cards.headline: No signposts at all?
cards.body: Plenty of arguments have none. Then fall back on Level 2's test: is someone trying to establish one statement as true by basing it on another? The claim being established is the conclusion. The others are premises, signposted or not.

title: The Unstated Premise
objective: After this level you can spot the hidden assumption an argument needs but never says out loud.
summary: Many arguments lean on a premise they never state. Find it by asking what else must be true, fill it charitably, and look hard at hidden 'should' premises.

cards.headline: "It's Monday, so the museum is closed." Something is missing.
cards.body: The argument works, but only thanks to a claim nobody said: the museum closes on Mondays. Like an iceberg, many arguments show only their tip. The part below the waterline is often the part that matters most.

cards.headline: The premise nobody said
cards.body: A missing, or unstated, premise is one an argument needs in order to work but never states. An argument with a part left unsaid even has a name: an enthymeme. Everyday talk is full of them. That's why logicians count making missing premises explicit as a central part of taking an argument apart.

cards.headline: How to find it
cards.body: Ask: what else would have to be true for the conclusion to follow? Then fill the gap with the most plausible claim that does the job. That's the principle of charity: rebuild the argument as strong as it can reasonably be. "The museum closes on Mondays" beats "Every building in town closes on Mondays".

mascot.line: Keep this: when an argument ends in "should", look for the hidden "should" it rests on.

cards.headline: Where arguments hide their values
cards.body: "This phone is cheaper, so you should buy it." The premise is a fact; the conclusion is a should. Arguments like that often rest on an unstated value judgment, Level 4 style: you should buy the cheaper phone. Say it out loud and you can finally question it. Cheaper, sure. But what about the battery?

title: Explaining Isn't Arguing
objective: After this level you can tell an explanation of why something happened from an argument that something is true.
summary: An argument tries to show that a claim is true; an explanation shows why something already accepted is true. Both can use 'because', so ask what job the words do.

cards.headline: "The grass is wet because it rained." Is that an argument?
cards.body: Now try: "It must have rained, because the grass is wet." Same two facts, same "because". But the first tells you why the grass is wet, and the second tries to convince you that it rained. One explains; the other argues.

cards.headline: That versus why
cards.body: An argument tries to establish that a claim is true. An explanation starts from something already accepted and shows why it's true. "The grass is wet because it rained" doesn't try to prove the grass is wet. You can see that for yourself. It tells you how it got that way.

cards.headline: Different jobs
cards.body: The two aim at different things. Explaining aims at understanding: the explainer assumes you already accept the fact. Arguing aims to make a claim acceptable to someone who doesn't accept it yet. So here's a quick check: is the claim in doubt? If everyone already agrees it's true, the "because" is probably explaining.

cards.headline: Why the difference matters
cards.body: Asked "Why did this metal expand?", you might answer: "It was heated, and all metals expand when heated." That explains; it doesn't prove the metal expanded. Mistake an explanation for an argument and you'll go hunting for proof nobody offered. And as Level 6 warned, "because" alone can't tell you which you're facing. The job it's doing can.

title: Arguments in Chains
objective: After this level you can trace how one argument's conclusion becomes the premise of the next.
summary: In an extended argument one step's conclusion becomes the next step's premise. Intermediate conclusions do both jobs; the main conclusion supports nothing further.

cards.headline: Lost keys: "Not in the kitchen, so they must be in the bedroom."
cards.body: Behind that sentence sits a small chain. I searched the kitchen and didn't find the keys, so they're not in the kitchen. They're either in the kitchen or the bedroom, so they're in the bedroom. The first step's conclusion has become the second step's premise.

cards.headline: Extended arguments
cards.body: Logicians call this an extended argument: at least one premise is itself backed by further reasons. "The keys aren't in the kitchen" isn't just asserted; it rests on the search. Real arguments very often have this shape, each step leaning on the one before, like a row of dominoes.

cards.headline: One claim, two jobs
cards.body: "The keys aren't in the kitchen" plays two parts. It's the conclusion of the search step and a premise of the bedroom step. A claim like that is an intermediate conclusion. Spotting them is how you see an argument's shape instead of a heap of sentences.

mascot.line: This makes the checkpoint easier: long arguments are short ones linked together. Check them one link at a time.

cards.headline: Finding the main conclusion
cards.body: The main conclusion is the claim at the end of the chain: it depends on the others but supports nothing further. Here, it's "the keys are in the bedroom". The kitchen step is a subargument, giving the main conclusion indirect support. So if the kitchen search was sloppy, the bedroom conclusion loses its footing too.

title: Deduction
objective: After this level you can explain deduction: reasoning in which true premises guarantee a true conclusion.
summary: In a deductive argument, true premises guarantee a true conclusion. Test the guarantee by hunting for a counterexample. Aristotle set deduction beside induction.

cards.headline: "Either the butler or the gardener did it. The butler didn't."
cards.body: You already know who did it. No fingerprints, no confession, and you don't even know what "it" was. Remember this pair from Level 5? If both premises are true, there's no way out: the gardener did it. That trapdoor feeling has a name, and it's this level's subject.

cards.headline: Premises that leave no way out
cards.body: That's deduction: reasoning in which the premises are meant to guarantee the conclusion. If the premises are true, the conclusion must be true too. Not probably. Must. The butler argument works that way. Grant that one of the two did it and that the butler didn't, and you've already granted that the gardener did. There's no room left for anyone else.

cards.headline: Hunting for a counterexample
cards.body: How do you check a guarantee? Look for a counterexample: a case where every premise is true but the conclusion isn't. Try this one: "If the driver did it, the maid didn't. The maid didn't do it. So the driver did it." Now picture a third person doing it. Both premises stay true, and the driver walks free. One case like that, and the guarantee is gone.

cards.fact: Aristotle split arguments into two kinds: deduction and induction.
cards.context: His word for deduction was sullogismos. Induction, epagoge, he described as argument from the particular to the universal: from the cases you've seen to a general rule. This chapter starts with the first kind, then turns to its rival.

title: Valid Doesn't Mean True
objective: After this level you can explain validity and why a valid argument can still reach a false conclusion.
summary: An argument is valid when true premises could not give a false conclusion. Validity comes from form, so a valid argument can have false premises and a false conclusion.

cards.headline: "Oranges aren't fruit, so they must be musical instruments."
cards.body: The full version: "Oranges are either fruit or musical instruments. Oranges are not fruit. So oranges are musical instruments." Ridiculous. Yet the logic textbook forall x holds it up as a valid argument. Nothing is wrong with the reasoning. Something is badly wrong with a premise.

cards.headline: What valid really means
cards.body: An argument is valid when it's impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false. That's the whole test. It doesn't ask whether the premises are true, only what would follow if they were. If oranges really were fruit or instruments, and really weren't fruit, they'd have to be instruments. The reasoning is airtight. The fruit bowl isn't.

cards.headline: It's all in the shape
cards.body: Validity comes from an argument's form, the skeleton left when you strip out the content. Every argument shaped "All A are B. No B are C. So no A are C." is valid, whatever A, B and C are. Content doesn't matter, so silliness doesn't either: "All toasters are made of gold. All gold things are time-travel devices. So all toasters are time-travel devices" is valid too.

cards.headline: True isn't enough either
cards.body: It works the other way round as well. "London is in England. Beijing is in China. So Paris is in France." Every sentence is true, yet the argument is invalid: nothing in the premises keeps Paris in France. Validity rules out just one mix, true premises with a false conclusion. Every other mix can turn up in a valid argument.

title: Soundness
objective: After this level you can explain why an argument needs both a valid form and true premises to be sound.
summary: A sound argument is valid and has all true premises, so its conclusion must be true. Rebut an argument by attacking a premise or its form; a flawed argument does not make its conclusion false.

cards.headline: "Every cookie in that jar is oatmeal raisin." You bite: chocolate chip.
cards.body: The reasoning looked perfect. Every cookie in the jar is oatmeal raisin; you took yours from the jar; so it's oatmeal raisin. The form is valid, Level 12 style. And yet here you are, chewing the evidence. Something went wrong, and it wasn't the logic.

mascot.line: Keep this: valid is about the shape. Sound is the shape plus true premises.

cards.headline: Sound: valid plus true
cards.body: A valid argument promises a true conclusion only if its premises are true. So logicians add a second test. An argument is sound when it's valid and all its premises are actually true. Pass both tests, and the conclusion must be true. The cookie argument passed the first test and failed the second: somebody slipped a chocolate chip cookie into the jar.

cards.headline: Two ways to push back
cards.body: So there are two ways to rebut an argument: show that a premise isn't true, or show that the conclusion doesn't follow. Logic itself only helps with the second. Whether a premise is true is usually a job for other tools, like research, science or, here, lifting the lid. Logic tells you which question to ask. The jar answers it.

cards.headline: A bad argument can still land on the truth
cards.body: One warning. An invalid argument, or a valid one with a false premise, can still have a true conclusion. Maybe your cookie really was oatmeal raisin after all. A flawed argument fails to prove its point; it doesn't prove the opposite. So catching a bad argument tells you about the argument. It doesn't yet tell you about the cookie.

learned: Sound: a valid form plus all true premises

title: The Syllogism
objective: After this level you can test an "all" and "some" argument of the kind Aristotle first studied, using overlapping circles.
summary: Aristotle's syllogism links two premises and a conclusion through three terms. Venn's overlapping circles test it: shade what's empty, mark what exists, and see whether the conclusion shows.

cards.headline: "All of Mia's cousins are musicians. Some musicians are left-handed."
cards.body: "So some of Mia's cousins are left-handed." Sounds reasonable. It's an "all" and "some" argument, the oldest kind that logic studied, and it hides a trap. Three circles will spring it.

cards.headline: Aristotle's all-and-some arguments
cards.body: Aristotle's logical works hold the earliest formal study of logic we have, and his most famous achievement there is the syllogism. It has two premises and a conclusion, built from exactly three terms. One, the middle term, appears in both premises; the conclusion joins the other two. In Mia's argument the middle term is "musicians", linking "cousins" to "left-handed".

cards.headline: Three circles
cards.body: In 1880 the English logician John Venn introduced diagrams of overlapping circles, and they make a handy test. Draw one circle per term. Shade any region the premises say is empty; put an X where they say something exists. Then look. If the picture already shows the conclusion, the syllogism is valid. If you'd have to guess, it isn't.

cards.headline: Where does the X go?
cards.body: Try Mia. "All cousins are musicians" shades the part of the cousins circle outside musicians. "Some musicians are left-handed" needs an X where musicians and left-handed overlap. Inside the cousins circle, or outside? The premises don't say. So the X sits on the line, and the conclusion isn't guaranteed. Invalid. Those left-handed musicians might all be strangers.

learned: Aristotle's syllogism: two premises, three terms

title: If This, Then That
objective: After this level you can use the two valid if-then forms: affirming the "if" part and denying the "then" part.
summary: An if-then statement links an antecedent to a consequent. Affirm the 'if' part and the 'then' part follows (modus ponens); deny the 'then' part and the 'if' part falls (modus tollens).

cards.headline: "If it's raining, the ground is wet." Two safe moves follow from that.
cards.body: An if-then sentence is a small machine. Feed it the right fact and it hands you a new one, guaranteed. Feed it the wrong one and it jams, which is the next level's story. First, the two moves that always work.

cards.headline: The two halves of an if
cards.body: An if-then sentence is called a conditional. The part after "if" is the antecedent; the part after "then" is the consequent. Notice what it doesn't say. "If it's raining, the ground is wet" doesn't claim it's raining, or that the ground is wet. It claims a link. And it's false in only one case: rain falls and the ground stays dry.

cards.headline: Move one: affirm the if part
cards.body: Add the if part as a fact: "It's raining." Now you may conclude the then part: "The ground is wet." Logicians call this modus ponens, Latin for the method of affirming. Every argument with this shape is valid, whatever the if and then parts are about. You make this move all day without naming it.

cards.headline: Move two: deny the then part
cards.body: Or add a denial of the then part: "The ground isn't wet." Now the if part must be false too: "It isn't raining." This is modus tollens, the method of denying, and it's just as valid. If it were raining, the ground would be wet. It isn't wet, so it can't be raining. It feels backwards, but it's airtight.

title: The Backwards If
objective: After this level you can spot the two tempting invalid if-then forms: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.
summary: Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent look like Level 15's safe moves but are invalid. Only affirming the 'if' or denying the 'then' is safe.

cards.headline: "If she's Brazilian, she speaks Portuguese. And she does!" Case closed?
cards.body: It feels like the last level's move. But the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy files this one under fallacies. Two if-then shapes look almost exactly like Level 15's safe moves, and both are broken. The fix is knowing which half of the if you're holding.

cards.headline: Affirming the then part
cards.body: The Brazil argument affirms the consequent: it treats a true then part as proof of the if part. The form is invalid, and it's often mistaken for modus ponens. The then part can come true for other reasons. Her Portuguese does suggest she might be Brazilian, so it's a clue. It's just weak evidence on its own, and no guarantee.

cards.headline: Denying the if part
cards.body: The mirror-image slip is denying the antecedent: treating a false if part as proof of a false then part. "If you pass all the exams, you pass the class. You didn't pass all the exams. So you fail." Not so fast. The rule says nothing about students who miss one; there may be other ways to pass. This one is often mistaken for modus tollens.

mascot.line: Keep this: affirm the if, or deny the then. Those are the only two safe moves.

cards.headline: Which half are you holding?
cards.body: So here's the whole map. Affirm the if part, or deny the then part: valid, every time. Affirm the then part, or deny the if part: invalid. When in doubt, hunt for a counterexample, Level 11 style. Can you picture the premises true and the conclusion false? A Portuguese speaker who isn't Brazilian does the job.

title: Induction
objective: After this level you can explain induction: reasoning from examples to a conclusion that is probable, not certain.
summary: Induction reasons from cases to a probable conclusion. It is graded strong or weak, not valid or invalid, and new premises can overturn it.

cards.headline: "It has snowed in Calgary every winter so far. So it will this winter."
cards.body: Would you bet on it? Almost certainly. Would you call it proof? The textbook forall x says no: the argument is invalid. That isn't a criticism. It's a different kind of reasoning, the kind you use whenever you trust tomorrow to behave like yesterday.

cards.headline: From cases to a conclusion
cards.body: This is induction, Aristotle's second kind of argument from Level 11: from the cases you've seen to a general rule. Its conclusion is meant to follow with high probability, not certainty. However many snowy winters pile up, a dry one stays possible, so the premises could all be true while the conclusion is false. Deduction says "must". Induction says "very likely".

cards.headline: Strong or weak, not valid or invalid
cards.body: So induction gets its own grades. Instead of valid or invalid, an inductive argument is strong or weak. A strong one's premises make its conclusion likely. "Every winter so far" makes a strong case for snow. "It snowed last winter" would make a much weaker one. The question shifts from "Is there any way out?" to "How good are the odds?"

cards.headline: New facts can flip it
cards.body: "Tweets is a healthy bird. Most healthy birds fly. So Tweets probably flies." Strong. Now add: Tweets is 6 feet tall and runs 30 miles an hour. Suddenly you're picturing an ostrich, and the conclusion collapses. New premises can defeat an inductive argument. A valid deduction can't be overturned by adding premises: it stays valid whatever you add.

title: The Black Swan Problem
objective: After this level you can explain why no number of confirming cases proves a generalization, while one counterexample can sink it.
summary: Europeans took 'all swans are white' as settled until black swans were seen in Australia in 1697. No pile of confirmations proves a generalization; one counterexample disproves it by modus tollens.

cards.headline: For the Roman poet Juvenal, a black swan was the rarest thing imaginable.
cards.body: Early in the second century CE the satirist Juvenal described a good wife as "a rare bird in the earth, and very like a black swan". The phrase stuck. For centuries, "black swan" meant something that defied belief. It was a safe joke, because everybody knew what swans looked like.

cards.headline: Induction's favorite example
cards.body: Europeans assumed, from what they had seen, that all swans were white. That's Level 17's induction: every swan observed was white, so every swan is white. As inductions go, it looked strong. Each new white swan felt like one more piece of proof.

cards.fact: In 1697 a Dutch expedition in Western Australia saw black swans.
cards.context: Willem de Vlamingh's crew named a river after them. His note on the birds is gloriously flat: "They are quite black." Centuries of confident swan reasoning, undone by some birds paddling on a river.

cards.headline: One swan beats a thousand
cards.body: Here's the lesson. To verify that all swans are white, you'd have to check every swan. To disprove it takes one black swan. And that disproof is pure deduction, Level 15's denying the then part: if all swans are white, this swan is white. It isn't. So not all swans are white. No pile of white swans can prove the rule; one black swan sinks it.

title: Reasoning Like a Detective
objective: After this level you can explain inference to the best explanation: choosing the account that best fits all the clues.
summary: Inference to the best explanation (abduction) picks the account that best explains every clue. Holmes called it deduction, but it gives no guarantee: true clues can still lead to a false conclusion.

cards.headline: "You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive."
cards.body: That's Sherlock Holmes, meeting Dr. Watson for the first time in A Study in Scarlet. Watson is astonished; nobody told Holmes a thing. Later Holmes lays out his reasoning. It's worth a close look, because it isn't quite what he calls it.

cards.headline: Clues in search of a story
cards.body: Holmes saw a man of a medical type with a military air: an army doctor. His face was dark but his wrists were fair, so he'd been somewhere tropical. He looked haggard, and held his injured left arm stiffly. Where could an English army doctor have seen hardship and been wounded? Afghanistan was the story that fit every clue.

cards.headline: The best explanation
cards.body: Philosophers call this inference to the best explanation, or abduction: you conclude that whatever would best explain the evidence is true. You do it at breakfast. A plate, crumbs, jam and an empty milk carton on the table? A housemate's midnight snack. A burglar who stopped for a bite would explain it too, just far less plausibly. The winner must explain every clue, and beat its rivals.

mascot.line: People mix these up all the time: if true clues could still lead to a false conclusion, it isn't deduction.

cards.headline: Not deduction, whatever Holmes said
cards.body: Holmes calls his method "the science of deduction". Scholars have long pointed out that most of his inferences are abduction instead. The difference matters. Deduction guarantees its conclusion; the best explanation can be wrong even when every clue is true. A detective who forgets that is one odd coincidence away from arresting the wrong person.

title: Checkpoint: Deduction and Induction

summary: Peirce's bag of white beans, rearranged three ways: deduction guarantees, induction makes probable, and hypothesis (abduction) makes a fair guess.

cards.headline: A handful of white beans on a table. Where did they come from?
cards.body: In 1878 the philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce imagined a room full of bags of beans. One bag holds only white beans, and a handful of white beans lies on the table. Peirce guessed the handful came from that bag. From one little scene he drew all three kinds of reasoning in this chapter.

items.label: Deduction
points: All beans from this bag are white
These beans are from this bag
So these beans are white

items.label: Induction
points: These beans are from this bag
These beans are white
So all beans from this bag are white

items.label: Hypothesis
points: All beans from this bag are white
These beans are white
So these beans are from this bag

cards.headline: How much each one promises
cards.body: Same three sentences, shuffled. Deduction runs from the rule to the result, and true premises guarantee it. Induction runs from cases to the rule, so it's only probable: one black bean would sink it, black-swan style. Hypothesis, which Peirce also called abduction, guesses the story behind what you see. He wrote: "As a general rule, hypothesis is a weak kind of argument."

title: What a Fallacy Is
objective: After this level you can explain what a fallacy is and why a bad argument can still feel convincing.
summary: A fallacy is an error in reasoning that seems better than it is. Aristotle compared it to fake silver. Feeling convincing isn't the same as holding up, and a fallacy doesn't make a conclusion false.

cards.headline: A mousetrap doesn't look like a trap. To the mouse, it looks like lunch.
cards.body: Bad arguments work the same way. They offer something that looks like a reason, and the mind takes the bait. This chapter is a field guide to the most common traps, starting with the question of what makes something a trap at all.

cards.headline: An error in reasoning
cards.body: A fallacy is a kind of error in reasoning: the reasons on offer don't really get you to the conclusion. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy adds a wry note. Fallacious reasoning should not be persuasive, but it too often is. That gap is the whole problem. If bad arguments sounded bad, nobody would need a field guide.

cards.headline: Fool's silver
cards.body: One handy working definition: a fallacy is an argument that seems better than it really is. Aristotle, whose Sophistical Refutations is the first known systematic study of fallacies, opened with a comparison. Some metal only seems to be silver or gold. Likewise, some reasoning only seems genuine, because the inexperienced see it only from a distance. Up close, the tin shows.

mascot.line: Keep this: "it feels convincing" and "it's a good argument" are two different tests. Fallacies pass only the first.

cards.headline: Convincing isn't the same as good
cards.body: Logic textbooks separate two kinds of pull. An argument can be psychologically compelling: it feels right, stirs you, fits what you hoped. Or it can be rationally compelling: its reasons actually hold up. A fallacy is an argument that fails the second test once you look carefully, even while it keeps passing the first.

cards.headline: A flaw, not a verdict
cards.body: One warning before the hunt. A fallacy is a flaw in the argument, not proof that its conclusion is false. Bad reasoning can still stumble onto the truth. So spotting a fallacy tells you to stop leaning on that argument. It doesn't tell you to believe the opposite.

title: Attacking the Person
objective: After this level you can spot an ad hominem, which attacks the arguer instead of the argument.
summary: An ad hominem ('to the person') attacks the arguer instead of the argument, in abusive or circumstantial form. A person's trustworthiness matters to testimony, not to an argument's reasons.

cards.headline: "Why listen to her about Kepler? She's only fifteen."
cards.body: That example comes from the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's list of fallacies. Notice what the reply never mentions: a single thing she actually said about Kepler's astronomy. It swings at her instead.

cards.headline: Aim at the arguer, miss the argument
cards.body: An ad hominem, Latin for "to the person", is an irrelevant attack on the person arguing, presented as if it sank the argument itself. Her age might make you wonder about her. It does nothing to her reasoning, which stands or falls on the evidence about Kepler. The punch lands, just on the wrong target.

cards.headline: Two common versions
cards.body: The abusive version points to an unflattering trait: "Ignore Tom's plan for the park; he once got a speeding ticket." The circumstantial version says the view comes from self-interest: "Of course the baker says bread is good for you." But a self-interested claim can still be sound. A motive is worth noticing. It isn't a rebuttal.

cards.headline: When the person does matter
cards.body: Not every personal point is a fallacy. In court, a lawyer may question a witness's honesty, because testimony is only as good as the witness's word. An argument is different: you can check its reasons yourself. So the hard part, and the test, is relevance. Does this fact about the person bear on the claim, or only on how you feel about them?

cards.fact: John Locke described the ad hominem in 1690. He didn't call it a fallacy.
cards.context: In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Locke described a family of "ad" arguments people use to win agreement, ad hominem among them. Labeling them fallacies was left to later writers. For Locke it meant pressing someone with their own earlier admissions; the personal-attack sense came later.

title: The Straw Man
objective: After this level you can spot a straw man, which knocks down a weaker version of someone's view instead of the real one.
summary: A straw man swaps someone's view for a weaker one they don't hold, knocks it down and claims victory. Two errors: it isn't their view, and beating it wouldn't beat theirs.

cards.headline: A scarecrow is shaped like a person. It's much easier to knock over.
cards.body: That's the trick behind one of the most common moves in any disagreement. Instead of taking on what someone actually said, you build a flimsier version of it, and knock that down instead.

cards.headline: Swap, then smash
cards.body: Maya: "The office should stock fewer sugary snacks." Leo: "So you want to ban all food at work? Absurd." Leo has built a straw man: a position that looks like Maya's but is far easier to refute, one she would never endorse. Then he knocks it down and acts as if her real view went down with it.

cards.headline: Two things go wrong
cards.body: First, Maya doesn't hold the view Leo attacked. Second, even if someone did, showing "ban all food" is silly says nothing about "fewer sugary snacks". The natural reply is the one Maya is already forming: "Wait! That's not what I said." And if Leo bent her words on purpose, it isn't just bad reasoning. It's lying.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Ad hominem hits the person. Straw man hits a fake copy of their view.

cards.headline: Person or position?
cards.body: Straw man and ad hominem are cousins: both are smears. Smear the opponent and you get an ad hominem; smear the opponent's argument and you get a straw man. Leo left Maya herself alone and bent her words instead. That's the straw man's signature.

title: The False Choice
objective: After this level you can spot a false dilemma that hides the options beyond the two on offer.
summary: A false dilemma offers too few options and demands a pick. Its flaw is a false premise: that these are the only choices. Escape by naming a missing option; a genuinely complete menu is fine.

cards.headline: A toaster with two settings: burnt and off.
cards.body: It's a joke because you know toasters do better than that. Arguments pull the same move with a straight face, and there it's no joke. Shrink the menu to two options, one of them awful, and you can steer someone to the one you wanted.

cards.headline: Too few options
cards.body: A false dilemma unfairly offers too few choices, then insists you pick one. With just two, it's also called a false dichotomy or the black-or-white fallacy. "Either you love this band or you have no taste" ignores liking a few of their songs, or just preferring jazz. The flaw sits in a premise: the claim that these are the only options.

cards.headline: Going between the horns
cards.body: One example in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy is a pollster asking whether your boss is drunk on the job once a week, twice a week or more. What about never? Picture the options as the horns of a charging bull. Name a choice the menu left out, and you slip between the horns, ungored.

cards.headline: Not every either/or is false
cards.body: Some choices really are two-way. "Will you give $20 or won't you?" is fair: those are the only options. So the test is whether the menu is complete, not whether it's short. A neat way to remember it: everything is either black or not black, but not everything is either black or white.

title: The Slippery Slope
objective: After this level you can judge a slippery slope argument by checking how likely each step really is.
summary: A slippery slope says one step leads step by step to disaster. It's a fallacy when that ending is exaggerated. Test each link; even likely links can make an unlikely chain. Some slopes are real.

cards.headline: "If Sam stays up late tonight, he'll never go to bed on time again."
cards.body: Next it's midnight every night, then he's asleep in class, then his grades collapse. One small step, one terrible ending. Arguments shaped like this can be right, or wildly wrong. This level is about telling which.

cards.headline: A chain of steps downhill
cards.body: A slippery slope argument says a first step will probably lead to a second, then a third, until something bad waits at the bottom. So, don't take the first step. The shape itself isn't a fallacy. It becomes one when the chance of reaching the bottom is exaggerated. When the steps are causes, it has a fitting nickname: the domino fallacy.

cards.headline: Test every link
cards.body: So check the steps one at a time. How likely is one late night to become a habit? A habit to failing school? There's a subtler catch, too. Even if every single link is fairly likely, the whole chain can still be unlikely. Each "probably" lets a little doubt in, and the doubts pile up by the bottom.

mascot.line: Keep this: judge the steps, not how scary the bottom looks.

cards.headline: Some slopes are real
cards.body: A slope isn't fallacious just because it ends somewhere bad. Whether it's a fallacy depends on how likely each step really is. If every step truly tends to follow the one before, the warning is fair. That's why shouting "slippery slope!" isn't an automatic win. You have to show which step slips.

title: Going in Circles
objective: After this level you can spot circular reasoning, where the conclusion is quietly assumed in the premises.
summary: Circular reasoning starts with what it wants to end with; begging the question hides the conclusion in a premise. Test: could the premise be accepted without the conclusion?

cards.headline: "You can trust my diary. Page one says everything in it is true."
cards.body: The diary vouches for the diary. It sounds like a reason, but follow it and you end up right where you started, like a snake swallowing its own tail.

cards.headline: Ending where you began
cards.body: Circular reasoning starts with what it's trying to end up with. Its tightest form is begging the question: a premise quietly assumes the conclusion. "Dana is the best captain, because no one leads better than Dana." The reason is just the claim in a new outfit. Good reasoning takes you somewhere new; this only repeats the point.

cards.headline: Small circles and big ones
cards.body: Imagine a dictionary that defines "endless loop" as "see loop, endless", and "loop, endless" as "see endless loop". Useless. Yet a whole dictionary is one giant circle of words defined by other words, and it's hugely informative. The fallacy is the small, tight circle that never lets any new information in.

cards.headline: The way out of the circle
cards.body: To catch a circle, ask of each premise: could someone who doesn't yet accept the conclusion still accept this? "Page one says it's true" only persuades someone who already trusts the diary. A premise you could defend on its own, without first accepting the conclusion, breaks the circle.

cards.fact: "Beg the question" is a 16th-century translation of Aristotle's petitio principii.
cards.context: Merriam-Webster says a better translation would have been "assume the conclusion". Today most people use "that begs the question" to mean "that raises the question", and that use is established too. In logic, though, it means the circle.

learned: Circular reasoning ends where it began
Begging the question hides the conclusion in a premise

title: The Red Herring
objective: After this level you can spot a red herring that changes the subject while seeming to answer it.
summary: A red herring is a digression that pulls a discussion off the issue, named for smelly smoked fish said to throw hounds off a trail. Test: is the original question any closer to settled?

cards.headline: "Did you finish your homework?" "Did anyone walk the dog today?"
cards.body: Smooth. The dog may well need a walk. But notice what just happened to the homework question: it vanished. That's a red herring, one of the smoothest ways to dodge a question without anyone noticing.

cards.fact: "Red herring" comes from smoked herring: red, and very smelly.
cards.context: Such fish, the story goes, were dragged across a trail to throw hunting dogs off the scent. In reasoning, a red herring is a digression that leads you off the track of what's relevant. A deliberate false lead in a crime investigation counts as one too.

cards.headline: How the switch works
cards.body: A red herring doesn't refute anything. It just moves the conversation somewhere else, ideally somewhere that feels nearby, so the jump seems natural. Homework and dog walks are both chores. But the question on the table was homework. The test is simple: after the reply, is the original question any closer to settled?

cards.headline: Winning the wrong argument
cards.body: A close cousin argues for something true but beside the point. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's example: the claim that Calgary is Canada's fastest-growing city isn't defeated by showing it isn't the biggest. That reply can be a perfectly sound argument. It's just about a different claim.

learned: A red herring leads away from the issue

title: "What About You?"
objective: After this level you can explain why pointing out someone's hypocrisy doesn't answer their argument.
summary: Tu quoque ('you too') rejects advice because the speaker doesn't follow it. Hypocrisy is a reason for suspicion, not a rebuttal. Its cousin: two wrongs don't make a right.

cards.headline: Your neighbor tells you to exercise regularly. She never does.
cards.body: Tempting reply: "Look who's talking!" It feels like a knockout. But ask yourself one thing. Does her skipping it make regular exercise any worse for you? This example comes from the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

cards.headline: "You too!"
cards.body: That reply has a Latin name: tu quoque, "you too". It rejects advice or an argument because the person giving it doesn't live by it. It's a kind of ad hominem, because the spotlight swings from the reasons to the person. As the Stanford Encyclopedia puts it, the value of advice isn't wholly dependent on the integrity of the advisor.

cards.headline: Suspicious, not refuted
cards.body: Hypocrisy isn't nothing. Catching someone who doesn't practice what they preach is a fair reason to look harder at what they say. It just isn't enough to throw it out. Her reasons for exercising are exactly as strong, or as weak, as they were before you noticed her couch.

cards.headline: Dodging with a counterpunch
cards.body: In a quarrel, tu quoque makes a handy escape hatch. Accused of leaving dishes in the sink, you fire back: "You left yours there yesterday!" Maybe true. But the accusation hasn't been answered, only returned. Its cousin, "two wrongs don't make a right", names the move of excusing a wrong because someone else did one first.

title: Everyone Believes It
objective: After this level you can explain why a claim's popularity is not, by itself, evidence that it is true.
summary: The appeal to the people and the bandwagon treat popularity as proof. What many believe is somewhat likely true, and reasoned agreement counts, but a headcount alone is overrated.

cards.headline: "You should turn to channel 6. It's the most watched channel this year."
cards.body: That example comes straight from the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's list of fallacies. All those viewers can't be wrong, can they? Maybe not about something. But are they right about what you would enjoy?

cards.headline: Counting heads isn't checking
cards.body: The appeal to the people, in Latin argumentum ad populum, treats "most people believe it" as if that settled the matter. It runs in reverse, too: "hardly anyone thinks that, so it's wrong." But agreeing with the crowd isn't a reliable sign of being right, and disagreeing isn't a reliable sign of being wrong.

cards.headline: Jumping on the bandwagon
cards.body: Its lively cousin is the bandwagon: believe it because more and more people are coming to. Picture the wagon where the band plays, and everyone climbing aboard without asking where it's headed. What's missing is any sign that the thing is popular because it's good.

cards.headline: When the crowd is a clue
cards.body: Popularity isn't worthless. What most people believe is, for that reason, somewhat likely to be true. And pointing out that many people studied a question and reached a reasoned answer isn't a fallacy at all. The mistake is overrating the headcount: treating "popular" as proof, instead of asking why people believe it.

title: Checkpoint: Classic Fallacies
objective: After this level you can name the classic fallacies and explain how each one dodges, distorts or assumes the point.
summary: A mascot debate full of fallacies, sorted into three families: dodging, distorting or assuming the point. Logicians group them too, and still dispute the details.

cards.headline: The school board is choosing a mascot: owls or foxes.
cards.body: Ana: "Owls. Every other school in the county picked owls." Ben: "Ana's kid is in the owl club, so ignore her." Cara: "So Ben thinks owls are worthless?" Dev: "It's owls or no mascot at all." Four speakers, four traps, and not one reason about which mascot is better. Time to use everything this chapter taught.

items.label: Dodges the point
points: Ad hominem: aims at the arguer
Tu quoque: "you too!"
Red herring: changes the subject

items.label: Distorts the point
points: Straw man: fights a weaker fake view
Slippery slope: exaggerates where steps lead
Popularity: overrates a headcount

items.label: Assumes the point
points: Circular: a premise restates the conclusion

cards.headline: Families, not fences
cards.body: Logicians group fallacies too. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes fallacies of relevance, which lean on an irrelevant reason, like the ad hominem, and fallacies of illegitimate presumption, like begging the question and the false dilemma. But researchers still dispute the best way to classify them. Treat any grouping as a guide, not a fence.

cards.fact: Most classic fallacies trace back to two books, by Aristotle and by John Locke.
cards.context: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations and Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) the two fountainheads of the core fallacies in logic textbooks. You've now met the ideas both of them started.

title: What Counts as Evidence
objective: After this level you can explain what makes something evidence for a claim rather than just a reason to like it.
summary: Evidence makes a claim more or less likely to be true, as smoke signals fire. Clifford's shipowner had reasons to like his belief, not evidence for it, and luck didn't excuse him.

cards.headline: A shipowner stopped worrying about his old ship. Then it sailed.
cards.body: In an 1877 essay, W. K. Clifford told of an owner who knew his emigrant ship was old and had often needed repairs. Refitting her would be costly, so he talked himself out of his doubts and came to feel sincerely sure she was safe. She went down in mid-ocean. What went wrong wasn't his sincerity. It was what his belief rested on.

cards.headline: Evidence points to the truth
cards.body: Evidence for a claim is something that makes the claim more likely to be true; evidence against makes it less likely. Philosophers' favorite picture is smoke. Smoke is evidence of fire, because it's a reliable sign of fire. It isn't evidence of rain, however much you'd like some rain. So the test for any reason is simple: does it make the claim more likely to be true?

cards.headline: Reasons to like a belief
cards.body: The shipowner had reasons, just the wrong kind. Believing his ship was sound spared him a costly, slow refit. Philosophers call reasons like that prudential: they're about what holding a belief does for you. Evidence is about whether the belief is true. A comfortable belief can be useful and still be false, and the ocean doesn't check your motives.

mascot.line: Keep this: ask what a reason says about the claim, not what believing it would do for you.

cards.headline: Clifford's verdict
cards.body: Clifford then changed the ending: suppose the ship arrived safely. Was the owner any less to blame? "Not one jot." He had got his belief by stifling his doubts, not by patient investigation, so he had no right to it either way. His famous rule: "It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence." Luck doesn't turn a wish into evidence.

title: Who Has to Prove It?
objective: After this level you can explain the burden of proof and why it falls on the person making the claim.
summary: Whoever makes a claim carries the burden of proof; 'prove I didn't' tries to shift it. Criminal courts put it on the prosecution, Roman law stated it in one line, and it binds critics too.

cards.headline: "My cat can predict rain." "Prove it." "You prove she can't!"
cards.body: Maya and Leo could go around like this all afternoon, each waiting for the other to do the work. Logic has a rule that settles who goes first. Once you know it, a lot of stalled arguments get unstuck.

cards.headline: The burden of proof
cards.body: Whoever makes a claim carries the burden of proof: it's their job to back it up. "You can't prove I didn't" doesn't meet that burden. It tries to shove it onto the listener. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls this a misplaced burden of proof, and its example fits Maya nicely: someone reports seeing a green alien and answers every doubt with "You can't prove I didn't."

cards.headline: Courts run on it
cards.body: Criminal trials put the rule to work. In the United States, the burden of proving a defendant's guilt is on the prosecution, which must establish it beyond a reasonable doubt. The defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty. So if the prosecution fails to prove guilt, the verdict is not guilty, even if the defense has offered no evidence of innocence at all.

cards.headline: An old rule that cuts both ways
cards.body: Roman law put it in one line: Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat. Proof lies on the one who asserts, not on the one who denies. And it applies to critics too. Call someone's reasoning a fallacy and you've made a claim of your own, so, the encyclopedia notes, the burden is on you to be able to give your reasons.

title: Not Found Isn't Disproved
objective: After this level you can explain when a lack of evidence counts against a claim and when it proves nothing.
summary: Taking 'not proved' as 'false' (or 'not disproved' as 'true') is the appeal to ignorance, named by Locke. Absence counts only after a thorough search that would have found the evidence.

cards.headline: "Nobody has shown my lucky charm doesn't work." So it works?
cards.body: It sounds almost fair: no one has proved it wrong. But turn it around. Nobody has proved it works, either. If "not disproved" meant true, the charm would work and not work at the same time. Something is off, and it has a name.

cards.headline: The appeal to ignorance
cards.body: Treating a lack of evidence as proof is the appeal to ignorance, also called the argument from ignorance. It comes in two forms: not knowing a claim is true is taken to prove it false, or not knowing it's false is taken to prove it true. Its Latin name, argumentum ad ignorantiam, comes from John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding of 1690.

mascot.line: People mix these up: "no evidence" after no search, and "no evidence" after a good one. Only the second one counts.

cards.headline: When absence does count
cards.body: Sometimes not finding something is good evidence it isn't there. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy sets two conditions: the search was thorough, and if the thing existed, there would be evidence to find. So ask two questions. Did anyone really look? And if it were there, would they have found it? Two yeses turn "no evidence" into evidence of absence.

cards.headline: Back in Level 9's kitchen
cards.body: Remember the lost keys? "I searched the kitchen and didn't find the keys, so they're not in the kitchen." That's an argument from absence, and it's only as good as the search. A glance at a cluttered counter proves little. Emptying every drawer proves a lot. Same words, very different evidence.

title: "It Worked for Me"
objective: After this level you can explain why one vivid personal story is weak evidence about what usually happens.
summary: An anecdote is one case offered as evidence about what usually happens. A healthy smoker fits research on tobacco's raised risk; only evidence that counts everyone shows what usually happens.

cards.headline: "My brother smokes, and he's never been sick a day in his life."
cards.body: So smoking can't really hurt you? That's close to word for word an example in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. The speaker has read the health warnings and knows about the research. One story about one brother still wins. Why does it feel so convincing, and why shouldn't it?

cards.headline: Anecdotal evidence
cards.body: A firsthand story offered as evidence about what generally happens is anecdotal evidence. The fallacy is leaning on a few such stories while discounting evidence gathered by systematic search or testing. The trouble is size. A story is one case. "Smoking can't hurt you" is a claim about what happens to everyone who smokes.

cards.headline: One lucky case fits the research
cards.body: The research says tobacco use is a leading cause of cancer and that people who use it have an increased risk of cancer. Increased risk isn't certainty. It means more smokers get sick, not that every smoker does. So a healthy brother doesn't contradict the research at all. Lucky exceptions are exactly what a raised risk leaves room for.

cards.headline: The question a story skips
cards.body: A story comes with a face and a happy ending. Systematic evidence comes with everyone else, including the people whose endings weren't happy. So when you hear "it worked for me", ask the question the story can't answer: what happened to all the others? Only evidence that counts them tells you what usually happens.

title: Jumping to Conclusions
objective: After this level you can spot a hasty generalization drawn from too few or unusual cases.
summary: A hasty generalization jumps from too few or unusual cases to a verdict about all. One rainy day in Flagstaff, one first day of class and a plate of edible plants show both failures.

cards.headline: One day in, a student decides the whole course will be boring.
cards.body: "Even though it's only the first day, I can tell this is going to be a boring course." That line is a textbook example, literally: Purdue University's Online Writing Lab uses it. One day of evidence, a verdict on a whole course. Reasoning from examples is fine. The problem is how few examples, and which ones.

cards.headline: Hasty generalization
cards.body: A hasty generalization is a conclusion based on insufficient or biased evidence: rushing to a verdict before you have the relevant facts. The bigger the claim, the more it needs. Meet two friendly people in Nicaragua and conclude everyone you meet there will be friendly? "All" leaves no room for error, so, as the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy points out, it would take meeting everyone.

cards.headline: Too few cases
cards.body: The first way to go wrong is too few cases. Matthew Van Cleave's open logic textbook imagines spending one day in Flagstaff, Arizona. It rains, so you conclude it rains there every day. A good generalization needs a large enough sample, and one day of weather says very little about a whole year of it.

cards.headline: Unusual cases
cards.body: The second way is unusual cases, a sample that isn't typical. Purdue's point about the first day is that it's usually full of housekeeping, so it's a poor preview of the course. Or take the encyclopedia's example: every plant on my plate is edible, so all plants are edible. The plants on a plate were chosen for being edible.

title: Cherry-Picking
objective: After this level you can spot cherry-picking, where only the evidence that helps the case is shown.
summary: Cherry-picking shows only the evidence that helps. A Colgate poster's '80% of dentists' left out that the survey let dentists recommend several brands. Accidental omissions count too.

cards.headline: A Colgate poster claimed: "More than 80% of dentists recommend Colgate."
cards.body: The number came from a real survey of dentists. Yet in 2007 Britain's Advertising Standards Authority ruled the poster misleading and told Colgate not to repeat the claim. Nobody said the figure was invented. The problem was what the poster left out.

cards.headline: Only the helpful evidence
cards.body: Cherry-picking means showing only the evidence that helps your case. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy files it under suppressed evidence: leaving out relevant information, usually the kind that counts against your conclusion. Every fact on display can be true. The trick is in which facts made it onto the display.

cards.headline: What the poster didn't say
cards.body: The survey let dentists recommend several toothpaste brands, not just one. The regulator found that readers would take the poster to mean 80% of dentists chose Colgate over every other brand, with the rest preferring something else. The survey never asked that. The same dentists could recommend rival brands too, and the poster didn't mention them.

cards.headline: Picked by accident
cards.body: Cherry-picking isn't always deliberate. The encyclopedia counts relevant evidence that's overlooked by accident as the same error, because either way the conclusion rests on part of the picture. So when a case looks spotless, ask two things: what would the full set of evidence show, and who chose the part I'm seeing?

title: Only the Survivors
objective: After this level you can explain survivorship bias, using the damaged planes that made it home from war.
summary: Abraham Wald saw that returning bombers showed only survivable damage, so armor belonged where they had the least. Survivorship bias: judging only what made it through a filter.

cards.headline: World War II bombers come home full of holes. Where do you add armor?
cards.body: The damage on returning planes looked like a map: the fuselage had taken far more hits than the engines. The obvious answer was to reinforce the most-hit spots, and military analysts planned to. A mathematician named Abraham Wald saw the flaw.

cards.headline: Look where the holes aren't
cards.body: Wald pointed out that the analysts were only looking at planes that had survived combat and returned. Planes hit in other places were missing from the count, most likely because those hits brought them down. So his advice ran the other way: add armor where the returning planes showed the least damage.

cards.headline: How we know
cards.body: Wald did this war work with the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, developing a method to estimate how vulnerable each part of a plane was. His memos were never published externally at the time. The Center for Naval Analyses reprinted them in 1980 under a title that says it all: estimating plane vulnerability based on damage of survivors.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: the evidence you can see already passed a filter. Ask what the filter removed.

cards.headline: Survivorship bias
cards.body: The error has a name: survivorship bias, paying attention only to what made it through some filter. It's why famous college dropouts who got rich can make a degree look pointless. You hear about them, not about the great majority of dropouts who don't become wealthy. Before you trust a pattern, ask: who never made it into this picture?

title: Extraordinary Claims
objective: After this level you can explain why a surprising claim needs stronger evidence than an ordinary one.
summary: Hume: proportion belief to the evidence; the more unusual a reported fact, the weaker a witness's word. Sagan popularized the slogan. Hume's frost example: a higher bar, not a closed door.

cards.headline: Your friend saw a cat on the roof. Fine. She saw a tiger on the roof. Hmm.
cards.body: Same friend, same eyesight, same roof. Yet the first report is easy to accept, and the second makes you want photos, paw prints and a call to the zoo. That isn't unfair to your friend. It's good reasoning.

cards.headline: Belief in proportion
cards.body: The Scottish philosopher David Hume put it in 1748: "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence." He added that the more unusual a reported fact is, the more a witness's word is weakened. It becomes a contest of two experiences: the testimony on one side, and everything you know about how things usually go on the other.

cards.headline: The slogan
cards.body: The astronomer Carl Sagan popularized the short version: "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence." He wasn't first. The sociologist Marcello Truzzi had written "an extraordinary claim requires extraordinary proof", and the mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace made the same point long before. A tiger on your roof isn't impossible. It's just up against everything you know about your street.

cards.headline: A higher bar, not a closed door
cards.body: Hume's own example shows the rule isn't a way to dismiss things. An Indian prince who refused to believe the first reports of frost, he said, reasoned justly: water turning solid lay far outside his experience, so he needed very strong testimony. And ice is real. An extraordinary claim can be true. It just has to clear a higher bar.

title: When Evidence Converges
objective: After this level you can explain why independent lines of evidence that agree are stronger than any one alone.
summary: Peirce: reasoning should be a cable of many fibers, not a chain. Whewell's consilience: evidence gains force when an idea fits cases of a different kind. The lines must be independent.

cards.headline: Did it rain last night? Wet streets. A full rain gauge. A log saying rain.
cards.body: Any one clue could fool you: a street cleaner, a sprinkler, a typo. All three together are hard to explain any other way. Why are several clues so much stronger than one, and when are they not?

cards.headline: A cable, not a chain
cards.body: In 1868 the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce wrote that reasoning should not form a chain, which is no stronger than its weakest link, but a cable whose fibers may be ever so slender, provided they are sufficiently numerous and intimately connected. A chain fails at its weakest step. A cable of evidence can lose a fiber and still hold.

cards.headline: Jumping together
cards.body: William Whewell called it a consilience of inductions, literally a "jumping together". Evidence is far more forceful, he said, when an idea explains cases of a different kind from the ones it was built on. His model was Newton's gravity: one law fit the moons of Jupiter, the planets and falling bodies.

cards.headline: Only if they're independent
cards.body: The fibers have to be separate. Clues count as different lines only if each could have failed on its own. Five friends repeating the same rumor are one line of evidence, told five times. That's why Whewell prized cases of a different kind: evidence from different places can't all share the same mistake.

title: Checkpoint: Weighing Evidence

summary: Carl Sagan's 1995 baloney detection kit, read as a map of the chapter: independent confirmation, the traps of ignorance, small numbers and selected evidence, and a warning about misuse.

cards.headline: The first tool
cards.body: The kit starts with things to do, and the first is: wherever possible, there must be independent confirmation of the "facts". That's Level 39's cable. One vivid story or one witness is a single fiber. Before you rank a claim as well supported, look for a second line of evidence that could have failed on its own.

title: What Makes a Cause
objective: After this level you can explain a cause as something that makes a difference: without it, the effect would not have happened.
summary: A cause makes a difference: take it away and the effect goes too. Hume said so in 1748, David Lewis built a theory on it, and courts use the same but-for test.

cards.headline: Your phone hit the floor at breakfast. By lunch it was dead. Guilty?
cards.body: Maybe the fall did it. Or maybe the battery was on its last legs anyway. Before you blame the floor, you need to know what a cause actually is. This chapter is about cause and effect, and it starts with a simple test: an imaginary rewind.

cards.headline: Hume's test: rewind without it
cards.body: In 1748 the philosopher David Hume defined a cause, then restated it in other words: a cause is something where, "if the first object had not been, the second never had existed." In plain terms: take the cause away and the effect disappears too. So rewind the morning, keep the phone safely in your pocket, and ask whether it still dies by lunch.

cards.headline: A cause makes a difference
cards.body: In 1973 the philosopher David Lewis built a whole theory of causation on Hume's second line. A cause, on his view, makes a difference, measured against what would have happened without it. Had the cause been absent, its effects would have been absent too. That's why "it would have died anyway" is such a strong reply. It says the fall made no difference, so it wasn't the cause.

cards.headline: Courts ask the same question
cards.body: Law uses this idea in both tort and criminal cases. To decide actual causation, courts apply the but-for test: but for X, would Y have occurred? The test has a weakness, though: alone, it reaches too far. Someone robbed on a detour around roadworks could call the mayor who promised the roadworks a but-for cause. For many, that link is too remote, so tort law also requires a closer, proximate cause.

title: Correlation Isn't Causation
objective: After this level you can explain why two things rising and falling together doesn't show that one causes the other.
summary: Two things can rise and fall together without one causing the other. Messerli's 2012 chocolate and Nobel prizes note made the point with a straight face.

cards.headline: Countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel prizes. Time for dessert?
cards.body: That was the finding of a short note in a leading medical journal in 2012, and the numbers were real. Switzerland topped both lists. Before you unwrap a second bar in the name of science, ask what a pattern like that can actually show.

cards.headline: Going together versus causing
cards.body: A correlation describes how two things vary together: how strongly, and in which direction. Causation is different: one event is the result of the other. Here's the catch. If A really causes B, the two will be correlated. But a correlation on its own is usually weak evidence that one thing causes the other.

cards.headline: The chocolate note
cards.body: Franz Messerli compared chocolate eaten per person with Nobel laureates per 10 million people in 23 countries and found a close correlation. Then he wrote the key line himself: a correlation between X and Y doesn't prove causation. It means X influences Y, Y influences X, or both are influenced by something underneath. Chocolate might sharpen minds. Or not.

mascot.line: Keep this: "goes together" and "causes" are two different claims. Check which one you've actually been shown.

cards.headline: A joke with a point
cards.body: The note ran in the journal's Occasional Notes section, a home for lighter pieces, and it was meant as a friendly reminder that over-reading correlations leads to wrong claims. Some journalists still treated the respected journal as a sign of quality. The lesson isn't that chocolate is useless. It's that "these go together" and "this causes that" are two different claims.

title: After This, So Because of This?
objective: After this level you can spot the post hoc fallacy, which treats "came first" as "caused it".
summary: Post hoc, ergo propter hoc: 'after this, therefore because of this'. Coming first is a clue, never proof, as the rooster and the lucky seat show.

cards.headline: Every morning the rooster crows. Then the sun comes up. Case closed?
cards.body: The order is perfect, day after day. Yet nobody thinks a bird hauls the sun over the horizon. So what exactly is wrong with the rooster's reasoning? And where do the rest of us make the very same move?

cards.headline: After this, therefore because of this
cards.body: Notice that B follows A, then hastily conclude that A caused B, and you've committed the post hoc fallacy. Its full Latin name is post hoc, ergo propter hoc: "after this, therefore because of this." It's one of the false cause fallacies. The rooster is the textbook case, because the only evidence offered is that the sunrise came after the crowing.

cards.headline: Why it's so tempting
cards.body: It feels right because causes really do come first: an effect never comes before its cause. And a pattern can be a genuine clue. Correlations are often good evidence of a causal link. So the mistake isn't noticing the order. It's the hasty jump from "came first" to "caused it" without checking anything else.

cards.headline: The lucky seat
cards.body: A basketball fan notices that every time he buys a good seat, his team wins, and every time he buys a cheap one, they lose. So the good seat must be causing the wins. It's an accidental pattern that tells him nothing about why the team wins, and it probably won't hold up. Still, a good seat is a good seat.

title: The Hidden Third Factor
objective: After this level you can explain how a confounder, like hot weather, can drive two things at once and fake a link between them.
summary: A confounder drives two things at once and fakes a link between them: hot weather behind ice cream and sunscreen, a cold behind sniffles and watery eyes.

cards.headline: Ice cream and sunscreen sales rise and fall together. Does one sell the other?
cards.body: Nobody buys sunscreen because they just had a cone. Yet the two climb and sink together across the year. Something else is pulling both strings, and once you see it, you'll start spotting it everywhere.

cards.headline: The factor behind both
cards.body: Australia's national statistics office uses exactly this example. Ice cream and sunscreen sales move together because of the season: hotter weather brings more of both. Neither causes the other. A hidden factor like the weather is called a confounder: something linked to both the supposed cause and the supposed effect, which distorts the link between them.

cards.headline: Sniffles and storms
cards.body: A runny nose goes with watery eyes, but neither causes the other: a cold causes both. In Iowa, summer lightning goes with bigger popcorn harvests, because storms bring the lightning and also the rain that grows the corn. Links like these are called spurious. When two things move together, ask whether a third thing is driving both.

cards.headline: Back to the chocolate
cards.body: Messerli weighed this reading of his chocolate data too. He found it hard to name one factor that could drive both chocolate eating and Nobel prizes over many years, though he allowed that differences in countries' socioeconomic status, geography and climate might play some role. That's the confounder question in action: before believing A causes B, look for the C behind both.
