title: From Study to Headline
objective: After this level you can explain how a cautious finding in one study can grow into a bold headline, and how to check it.
summary: Findings often grow on the way from study to press release to headline: stronger advice, causes from correlations, and human claims from mouse studies. Check the study upstream.

cards.headline: In 2019, a Twitter account began answering health headlines with two words.
cards.body: The words were "IN MICE". The researcher James Heathers started @justsaysinmice to add what exciting headlines had left out: the result came from a study of mice. He said it had a serious point but was supposed to be funny. It works because the missing words change everything.

cards.headline: A chain of retellings
cards.body: Between a study and your screen there are usually two retellings: a university press release, then the news stories written from it. In 2014, Petroc Sumner's team compared the two and found that exaggeration in health news was strongly tied to exaggeration in the press releases. Most of it was already there before a journalist touched it.

cards.headline: Three ways a finding grows
cards.body: Sumner's team tracked three kinds of stretch: advice stronger than the study gave, claims of cause drawn from research that only found a link, and conclusions about people drawn from animal studies. When a release stretched a finding, the news usually did too. When it didn't, news exaggeration was far rarer.

cards.headline: Where "in mice" goes missing
cards.body: A 2021 study in PLOS Biology found that when researchers leave the species out of a paper's title, news writers tend to do the same. Mouse studies are an important step in research, but their results often don't translate to people. So go upstream: find the study, and ask who or what was studied, and whether it showed a cause or only a link.

learned: Most news exaggeration starts in press releases

title: Echo Chambers
objective: After this level you can explain how hearing only agreeing sources makes a view feel more certain than the evidence allows.
summary: In an epistemic bubble, other voices are left out; in an echo chamber, they're actively discredited. Copies of the same agreement inflate confidence without adding evidence.

cards.headline: Would five copies of today's paper make you surer it's right?
cards.body: Obviously not: it's the same paper, five times. The philosopher C. Thi Nguyen borrows this picture from Wittgenstein, because it explains something less obvious. A feed full of agreement can make you far more confident than the evidence allows.

cards.headline: The bubble: voices left out
cards.body: Nguyen defines an epistemic bubble as a network where other relevant voices have been left out, perhaps by accident. Maybe your feed just shows people like you. Inside, agreement shows up far more often than it should, and it's tempting to grow surer with each echo. But agreement from a group you picked for agreeing shouldn't raise your confidence at all.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Bubble: the other side is missing. Chamber: the other side is there, and distrusted.

cards.headline: The chamber: voices discredited
cards.body: An echo chamber is different. Other relevant voices aren't just missing; they have been actively excluded and discredited, and members are brought to distrust every outside source. A bubble lacks information. A chamber has a reason ready to reject it.

cards.headline: Why it matters which one you're in
cards.body: Nguyen notes that bubbles pop easily: show members what they missed. Echo chambers can do the opposite, since meeting contrary views can raise members' trust in their insiders. Nobody is immune, including you: fan groups, hobby forums and friend chats can all drift this way. The test is simple to say and hard to do. When did you last take an outside source seriously?

Bubble: other voices left out
Echo chamber: other voices discredited

title: A Real Photo, the Wrong Story
objective: After this level you can explain why a real photo or video proves only what it shows, and check whether it is being used out of context.
summary: A genuine photo proves only what the camera saw. Lunch Atop a Skyscraper is real but staged; false context pairs real images with false claims, so check a photo's first appearance and caption.

cards.headline: 11 ironworkers eat lunch on a beam 850 feet above Manhattan. It's real.
cards.body: The famous photo was taken on September 20, 1932, on the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center, and the men were building it. It isn't a trick. It still doesn't show what most people think it shows.

cards.headline: Real, and staged
cards.body: Filmmakers who traced the original glass plate negative confirmed the photo is real, not a darkroom trick. But Smithsonian magazine calls it a daring publicity stunt. The men humored a photographer drumming up excitement about the building's near completion; some tossed a football, and a few pretended to nap. Both are true: a genuine photo of a staged moment.

cards.headline: What a photo can prove
cards.body: A photo shows what was in front of the camera at one moment. It doesn't show when, where or why, or what happened just outside the frame. Those come from the words around it. The misinformation researcher Claire Wardle names the trick that exploits that gap: false context, when genuine content is shared with false contextual information.

cards.headline: Check the caption, not just the pixels
cards.body: Wardle notes that misleading posts often don't fabricate anything; they reframe genuine content, so the context, not the content, is the weapon. So check the claim riding on the image. When and where did it first appear, and with what caption? A photograph can be a primary source, and like any primary source, its original record is where the real story starts.

title: Checkpoint: Judging Sources and Claims
objective: After this level you can decide how much to trust a claim by weighing who says it, what backs it and what else could explain it.
summary: The Cottingley fairy photographs weighed with this chapter's tools: who vouched for them, what the experts actually judged, and which explanation assumed less.

cards.headline: In 1920, Sherlock Holmes's creator vouched for photos of real fairies.
cards.body: In July 1917 Elsie Wright photographed her cousin Frances Griffiths with dancing fairies by a stream in Cottingley, West Yorkshire. Arthur Conan Doyle, long interested in spiritualism, endorsed the photos as genuine in the 1920 Christmas issue of The Strand Magazine. Let's weigh them with this chapter's tools.

cards.headline: What the experts actually said
cards.body: The photography expert Harold Snelling declared the negatives entirely genuine, with no trace of card or paper models. Two experts at Kodak found no flaw but refused to testify that they were genuine. Doyle printed both in his 1922 book. Notice what was being judged: negatives, not fairies. Doyle, a writer, made the leap himself.

cards.headline: Which explanation assumes less?
cards.body: Two explanations fit the pictures: real fairies, or paper figures posed by two girls. One needs a new kind of creature. In 1983 Elsie wrote a letter of confession. The fairies were drawings copied from Princess Mary's Gift Book, with wings added, held upright with hatpins. Snelling was right about the negatives, and wrong about what was in front of the camera.

title: Good Decision, Bad Outcome
objective: After this level you can explain why a decision should be judged by what was known at the time, not only by how it turned out.
summary: A good decision can end badly. Outcome bias judges choices by their endings; the fair test asks what was known at the time, as Hume's June-week forecaster shows.

cards.headline: The forecast said sun, so you left the umbrella. It poured. Bad call?
cards.body: You got soaked, so it feels like a mistake. But was the decision bad, or just the luck? Those are two different questions. Mixing them up is an easy slip, whether you're judging your own choices or anyone else's.

cards.headline: Judged by the ending
cards.body: The slip has a name: outcome bias. The same decision gets rated better when it turns out well than when it turns out badly. The researchers Baron and Hershey described it in 1988, and people show it even when they say outcomes shouldn't count. The ending is loud. The reasoning behind the choice is quiet.

mascot.line: Keep this: judge the choice by what was known then. Judge the luck separately.

cards.headline: The fair test: what was known then
cards.body: The fix is to judge a decision on the information the decision-maker had at the time, not on what happened next. Outcomes can have little to do with the quality of a choice. So ask: given what they knew then, were the reasons good? A sensible choice can end badly, and a reckless one can get lucky.

cards.headline: Hume's June and December
cards.body: In 1748 the philosopher David Hume made the point with the weather. Someone who expects better weather in any week of June than in one of December, he wrote, reasons justly. Yet they may still turn out mistaken. And when they do, they have no cause to complain of experience: it had already told them the weather was uncertain. Good reasoning, rained-out week.

title: The Sunk Cost Trap
objective: After this level you can explain why money or time already spent should not decide what you do next.
summary: A sunk cost is already spent whichever way you choose, so only what lies ahead should decide. Its pull is strong, and it often rests on an unstated premise.

cards.headline: You paid for the concert. It's pouring and you have a cold. Go anyway?
cards.body: Plenty of people would drag themselves out, so the money isn't "wasted". But look closely: the money is gone whether you go or not. This level is about why that matters for every choice you make next.

mascot.line: People mix this up: the cost was real. It just can't be a reason anymore.

cards.headline: Spent is spent
cards.body: A sunk cost is one you can't avoid because it has already happened. An accounting textbook puts the rule bluntly: a sunk cost won't change whichever option you pick, so it has no bearing on the decision. The concert ticket is sunk. The only live question is whether tonight is better in the rain or on the sofa.

cards.headline: The old car
cards.body: OpenStax's accounting textbook gives an example. Last year you spent $1,600 on car repairs. Now you must choose between repairing it again and trading it in. That $1,600 shouldn't count in the choice: it's spent whichever way you go. What counts is what each option costs and brings from here on.

cards.headline: Why it pulls so hard
cards.body: People show a greater tendency to keep going with something once money, effort or time has gone into it: the sunk cost effect. Part of the pull, the textbook notes, is that letting go means admitting a decision went wrong. Try Level 7's hidden-premise test on "I paid, so I should go." It needs "money already spent should decide what I do next". Said out loud, that wobbles.

title: Thinking One Step Further
objective: After this level you can use second-order thinking to spot the side effects and knock-on effects of a decision.
summary: Every act sets off a series of effects, and only the first is easy to see. Bastiat's seen and unseen, and Merton's warning about fixing on the immediate result.

cards.headline: A café offers free refills to win customers. Then what?
cards.body: The first effect is easy to picture: happy customers. But effects keep coming. Maybe people linger over their cups, tables stay full, and the lunch crowd can't find a seat. Thinking one step further means asking what the first effect sets off.

cards.headline: The seen and the unseen
cards.body: In 1850 the French economist Frédéric Bastiat wrote that an act produces not one effect but a series of effects. Only the first is immediate, so it is seen. The others arrive later; they are not seen, and we're fortunate if we foresee them. The bad economist, he said, looks only at the visible effect. The good one also weighs the effects that must be foreseen.

cards.headline: Sweet now, bitter later
cards.body: Bastiat said the same goes for habits: often, the sweeter a habit's first fruit, the more bitter the later ones. He named two teachers. Experience teaches brutally: you learn that fire burns by getting burned. Foresight is gentler. Second-order thinking picks foresight, looking past the immediate result by asking one question: "And then what?"

cards.headline: Why we stop at step one
cards.body: In 1936 the sociologist Robert K. Merton listed reasons actions have consequences nobody planned. One he called the "imperious immediacy of interest": caring so much about the immediate result you foresee that you never consider the further effects of the same act. The more you want the first effect, the less you look past it.

title: Imagine It Failed
objective: After this level you can run a pre-mortem: imagine a plan has already failed, then work out why, to find its weak points in advance.
summary: Gary Klein's pre-mortem: before a project starts, assume it has already failed and have everyone write down why, so weak points surface while they can be fixed.

cards.headline: Picture it: months from now, your plan has flopped. What went wrong?
cards.body: A strange question to ask before you've even started. But answering it, in detail, is exactly how a pre-mortem finds a plan's weak spots while there's still time to fix them.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the steps. Remember the twist: ask "why did it fail?", not "what might go wrong?"

cards.headline: A post-mortem, in advance
cards.body: The decision researcher Gary Klein described the pre-mortem in Harvard Business Review in 2007. A post-mortem finds out why a patient died; everyone learns something except the patient. A pre-mortem comes at the start of a project instead, so the plan can be improved rather than autopsied. The team assumes the project has already failed and asks what did go wrong.

cards.headline: How it runs
cards.body: The leader announces that the project has failed spectacularly. Everyone spends a few minutes writing down, alone, every reason they can think of, especially the ones they'd normally keep quiet about. Then people read out one reason each, in turn, until all are recorded, and the plan is strengthened. The real gift: it makes it safe for worried people to speak up.

cards.headline: The laptop problem
cards.body: In one session, on software for military air-campaign planners, a team member who had been silent through a long kickoff meeting spoke up. One algorithm wouldn't fit easily on the laptops used in the field, so it would take hours to run. The developers had already built a shortcut they'd been reluctant to mention. It went in, and the project succeeded.

title: How Sure Are You?
objective: After this level you can explain calibration: matching how confident you feel to how often you turn out to be right.
summary: Calibration: whether your confidence matches how often you turn out right. It can be off in several directions, and checking it needs a scored record, as IARPA's forecasting tournament showed.

cards.headline: Two friends both say "I'm sure" a lot. One is usually right. One isn't.
cards.body: They sound equally confident, so how would you know which one to trust? You'd have to keep track. That is the idea behind calibration, and it works on the confident voice in your own head too.

cards.headline: Confidence that matches the record
cards.body: Researchers call it calibration: whether the confidence you attach to your predictions matches how often those predictions come true. If you're well calibrated, the things you feel very sure about come true very often, and the things you feel unsure about come true less often. Your sense of sureness becomes a gauge you can actually read.

cards.headline: Ways to be off
cards.body: Miscalibration comes in more than one shape. Your confidence can run consistently too high, or too low. Or your judgments can be too extreme, leaping to near-certain yes or no, or too timid, hugging the middle. Overconfidence is the best-known form, and psychologists study it in depth. Your job is simpler: notice which way you lean.

cards.headline: Keeping score
cards.body: You can't check calibration without a record. In 2011, IARPA, the US intelligence community's research agency, launched a public forecasting tournament. Teams answered about 500 questions over four years and were eliminated if they missed accuracy benchmarks. After two years one team remained: Good Judgment, led by Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School.

title: Changing Your Mind
objective: After this level you can update a belief in proportion to new evidence, rather than all at once or not at all.
summary: Belief comes in degrees. Hume's rule, proportion your belief to the evidence, plus open-mindedness: suspend judgment when evidence is thin, take a position when it is enough.

cards.headline: New evidence arrives. Do you flip, dig in, or shift a little?
cards.body: Say you've always heard a bakery makes the best croissants in town, and a friend tells you hers was stale. Throwing out your belief would be too much. Ignoring your friend would be too little. This level is about the space in between.

cards.headline: Belief comes in degrees
cards.body: In his 1748 Enquiry, the philosopher David Hume noticed that when we reason about matters of fact, there are all degrees of assurance, from the highest certainty down to the weakest evidence. Belief isn't an on-off switch. It works more like a dial, and the evidence should set how far it turns.

cards.headline: Proportion your belief
cards.body: Hume's rule follows. When evidence points both ways, weigh the opposing cases, lean toward the side with more support, and hold that view with doubt and hesitation. One stale croissant nudges the dial. A dozen friends with stale croissants should turn it a long way.
cards.callout: Hume: "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence."

cards.headline: Open, not empty
cards.body: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy counts open-mindedness among a critical thinker's habits: being willing to re-examine a question you've already answered, if further evidence or reasoning might change your answer. Its partner habit is suspending judgment when the evidence is insufficient and taking a position once it's enough. Changing your mind, in proportion, is the point.

title: The Steel Man
objective: After this level you can build the strongest version of a view you disagree with before you answer it.
summary: A steel man is the strongest version of a view you disagree with. Mill's case for it: know the other side at its most persuasive, from people who believe it.

cards.headline: Before you argue against a view, could you argue for it?
cards.body: Try it with something small. Your sister insists pineapple belongs on pizza. Could you make her case so well that she'd nod along? If not, you may be about to beat a scarecrow she never built.

cards.headline: Straw versus steel
cards.body: A steel man is a strong version of an opposing view, set up to test your own. The word was coined in the 2010s as an answer to "straw man", the flimsy version that's easy to knock down. Straw is weak. Steel isn't. Building a steel man means answering the best case for a view, not the worst.

cards.headline: Mill's warning
cards.body: In On Liberty, published in 1859, John Stuart Mill put it sharply: "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that." If you can't answer the other side's reasons, or don't even know what they are, you have no ground for preferring either opinion. The orator Cicero, Mill noted, studied his opponent's case as intensely as his own.

cards.headline: Hear it from a believer
cards.body: Mill set a demanding bar. Hearing the other side from your own teachers, along with their rebuttals, isn't enough. You must hear it from people who actually believe it and defend it in earnest, and know it in its most plausible and persuasive form. That's a steel man: the other view at full strength, before you answer it.

title: Myths About Logic
objective: After this level you can debunk myths about logic, like "a fallacy proves the conclusion false" or "you can't prove a negative".
summary: Two myths about logic: a fallacy proves the conclusion false (the fallacy fallacy), and you can't prove a negative (folk logic, as Steven Hales showed).

cards.headline: "Your argument has a fallacy, so you're wrong!" Case closed?
cards.body: Not so fast. Logic has its own myths, and some of the most repeated ones get logic backwards. Here are two worth retiring.

mascot.line: Keep this: a fallacy sinks the argument, not the conclusion.

cards.headline: Myth 1: a fallacy proves the conclusion false
cards.body: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning. When an argument commits one, it fails to support its conclusion, and that's all you've learned. Spotting it gives you no reason, by itself, to reject the conclusion; there may be good arguments for it elsewhere. Leaping from "bad argument" to "false conclusion" is a fallacy of its own: the fallacy fallacy.

cards.headline: Bad reason, open question
cards.body: Imagine someone insists the café is open because they dreamed it. Terrible reason. The café might still be open. As one logic textbook puts it, reasonable people won't want to believe false things for bad reasons, or true things for bad reasons. So reject the argument, then check the claim on its own.

cards.headline: Myth 2: you can't prove a negative
cards.body: In 2005 the philosopher Steven Hales called this folk logic, not logic. A real law of logic is itself a negative: the law of non-contradiction says nothing is both true and false, and it can be proved. Any claim can be restated as a negative too: prove you exist and you've proved you aren't nonexistent. Evidence rarely gives certainty, but that's just as true of positive claims.

title: Your Thinking Toolkit
objective: After this level you can run a new claim through the tree's key checks: the argument, the evidence, the cause, your own biases and the source.
summary: Dewey's disordered rooms show the toolkit at work: rival explanations, tests, then belief. The SEP's checklist and a check on your own bias complete it.

cards.headline: You come home. Your things are thrown everywhere. What happened?
cards.body: John Dewey used exactly this scene in How We Think, back in 1910. Remember him from Level 1? Follow what his man does next, and you'll see the thinking toolkit at work in one messy room.

cards.headline: Two stories, held open
cards.body: Dewey's man first thinks: burglary. Then a second explanation occurs to him. His children are mischievous, and they may have thrown things about. That rival explanation stops him from accepting the first idea dogmatically. Judgment is held in suspense.

cards.headline: Test, then believe
cards.body: If burglars did it, valuables would be missing. He checks a box: some things are gone, but he might have moved them himself, so that test isn't decisive. Then the silver in the sideboard, which the children wouldn't take: all gone. Windows and doors show signs of tampering. Only now does belief settle on burglary.

cards.headline: The checklist
cards.body: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy suggests picturing critical thinking as a checklist, used in any order, selectively and more than once. Items include laying out possible solutions, deciding which evidence is relevant, judging the credibility of what others tell you, and accepting only what the evidence adequately supports. For a new claim: what's the argument, and its hidden premise? What's the evidence? What else could explain it? Who says so?

cards.headline: Check yourself too
cards.body: The last check points inward. People seek and interpret evidence in ways that favor what they already believe, often without noticing: confirmation bias. One remedy the encyclopedia names is holding off on a favorite explanation until the evidence rules out the others. That's just what Dewey's man did.
